entry.title: SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment – Pre-Upgrade Option for Release 2611
entry.content:
Overview

Providing a significant number of new features is an important goal of release upgrades to deliver innovations to our customers and partners. There are four major release upgrades per year following a predefined schedule as described in this blog post.

An upgrade is intended as a “no event” for customers and partners. For example, only compatible changes of released objects (APIs) will be delivered. We recommend performing a test of the custom-built productive apps in a test environment for the new release. The complexity of the technical dependencies between the custom-built apps and the underlying environment cannot be tested isolated, only including the ABAP environment on SAP-side. Therefore, we offer you to pre-upgrade selected systems 29 days in advance to test the applications prior to the planned standard-upgrade. Each ABAP environment release is connected to a fixed UI5 major version. As a consequence, the pre-upgrade tests include the upcoming UI5 version as well. Please refer to this blog post for further details.   

 

Purpose

This option enables a customer or partner to test the applications they have already developed on top of the new release a couple of days before the standard-upgrade. With SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment (aka "Steampunk"), we follow the approach of keeping released objects stable and provide all enhancements in a compatible fashion. Early testing is an additional measure to ensure proper software quality and might be used to detect unforeseen regressions. However, this option is not intended to test new features or to consume new features earlier.

 

Approach

The standard-upgrade of all systems to release 2611 is planned for November 13/15 (UTC).

A customer or partner can nominate one or more already existing systems for the pre-upgrade. A nominated system will be upgraded on October 16 within a planned downtime from 8:00 to 16:00 CET. Depending on the system settings, the actual technical downtime might be only ~20 min within the mentioned timeframe. Please refer to this blog post about the downtime-optimized upgrade. 

We recommend nominating a non-development system, such as a test system. The nomination of a development system is technically also possible, but fixes or other changes must not be imported into another system with a lower release. The nomination of a productive system doesn’t make sense because the purpose of the pre-upgrade is the re-test of the existing application before the productive system gets the new release.

According to the approach explained above, this offer is only relevant for customers or partners having at least two systems.

There might be situations where a correction of custom objects needs to be deployed. Such corrections are possible if the development / correction system is on the older release and is imported into the pre-upgraded system with the higher release.

Except potential fixes, the pre-upgrade is based on the same version as the standard-upgrade. It is planned to perform the pre-upgrade based on hotfix collection 2. The pre-upgrade systems will get potentially additonal patches after 2 weeks in the middle of the entire pre-upgrade test phase. It is planned to perform the standard-upgrade based on hotfix collection 3 and import the hotfix collection 3 to the pre-upgrade systems prio to the upgrade weekend on November 13.

 

Considerations for Partners and Add-On Development

With reference to the system landscape required for developing and operating Add-On deliveries (see documentation), pre-upgrading only the test systems — the test system for development (TST) and the test system for corrections (QAS) — is the recommended approach:

  • Development (DEV) and correction (COR) systems may also be pre-upgraded; however, no new release features should be used until the standard upgrade has been applied to all systems, as doing so would prevent a successful delivery.
  • The build system (BLD) must not be pre-upgraded, since any Add-On built on it can only be deployed to systems running a release equal to or greater than the one used during the build. Note that transient build systems carry an inherent risk: in the 2-3 days window leading up to the standard upgrade, newly provisioned transient build systems already run the new release, meaning any Add-On built during that period will only be deployable on systems that have already been upgraded. To avoid this risk, a permanent build system with hibernation is the recommended alternative.
  • The integration test system (ATI) is provisioned automatically during each product version build and is therefore not relevant for pre-upgrade planning.
  • Production systems (AMT) are not intended to be pre-upgraded, as the purpose of a pre-upgrade is to validate the new release in a non-productive environment without any impact on live operations.

 

Costs

This offering is optional and free of any additional charges.

 

Planned New Features

The planned new features will be published on the What's New for SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment on October 9. This list gives you an overview of potential areas for re-testing. The purpose of the pre-upgrade is not to consume these features before the standard-upgrade, because the documentation on help.sap.com will be delivered later before the standard-upgrade. It would also not be possible to transport code of such an adoption, because subsequent systems are not yet on the new release during the pre-upgrade phase.

Independent of the upgrades of the ABAP environment, we recommend developing automated tests for the custom-built apps to detect regressions early on and without manual effort for re-testing. Such automated tests are perfectly suited to be run in the pre-upgrade test phase.

 

Time Schedule

The following figure summarizes the general approach:

Milestones for release 2611:

  • September 15: Nomination of system(s) is possible in the Landscape Portal
  • October 9: Announcement of the planned new features
  • October 12: Pre-upgrade systems are known
  • October 16: Pre-upgrade (with hotfix collection 2)
  • October 30: Import of additional patches of hotfix collection 2 into pre-upgrade systems
  • November 11: Potential decision to postpone the upgrade
  • November 13: Import of hotfix collection 3 into pre-upgrade systems
  • November 13/15: Standard-upgrade (with hotfix collection 3)

 

System Nomination

To nominate a system, please register the system(s) by October 12 (EOB) latest by using the Landscape Portal. You can find further information about Accessing the Landscape Portal and about Manage SAP System Upgrade. Please do not create customer tickets for system nomination like in previous pre-upgrades.

With such a nomination, the customer agrees to an extraordinary planned maintenance on October 16 for the pre-upgrade and on October 30 and November 13 for the import of hotfix collections resp. additional patches (see above). You can find information about the required system downtimes in this blog post.

 

Report an Issue

Issues should be reported as part of the regression test phase by October 30 (EOB) to allow for a sufficient time frame for issue analysis and potential corrections on SAP-side.

Please create a customer ticket by using component BC-CP-ABA.

If a detected issue is likely to endanger the productive use after the standard-upgrade, you should use ticket priority very high despite the fact that the pre-upgrade system is not a productive system.

 

Exceptional Process in Case of Unresolved Priority Very High Issues

In case of the aligned decision on Wednesday, November 11 (based on unresolved priority very high tickets) to postpone the upgrade, a dedicated mitigation process needs to be started together with the respective customer or partner, with the following boundary conditions:

  • Resolving the open priority very high issues remains the highest priority for both, SAP and the customer or partner, as it is also the prerequisite for the upgrade.
  • According to the estimated issue resolution, catching up the upgrade needs to be planned.
  • The upgrade leads to a business downtime. Please refer to this blog post.
  • The upgrade must be scheduled within 7 calendar days the latest after fixing all remaining open priority very high issues.
  • We will not provide any fixes for the old release after the original date of the standard-upgrade to the new release.

In case business-critical issues are detected after the upgrade:

  • Issues need to be reported as priority very high issues and will be processed accordingly.
  • Going back to the release before upgrade is not an option. Therefore, resolving the issues in the new release with the appropriate priority is the required approach.

 

Summary

We recommend performing regression tests in pre-upgraded test systems to avoid day-1 impacts of productive custom apps after the standard-upgrade.

entry.title: Inside the S/4HANA Custom Code Migration Agent: A Technical Walkthrough (Series 3, Part 3)
entry.content:
Inside the S/4HANA Custom Code Migration Agent: A Technical Walkthrough

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 3 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: This part covers the real prerequisites, the exact workflow, and where SAP itself says the agent should not be trusted to decide alone.

Series Context

Part 2 was the manual path. This part is what SAP automated — same underlying ATC mechanics, now orchestrated by an agent that knows when to stop and ask.

SECTION 1 — PREREQUISITES: WHAT YOU ACTUALLY NEED INSTALLED

This is a real setup checklist, not a "just enable AI Core" wave-of-the-hand:

  • SAP S/4HANA target system running at least version 2023
  • SAP Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities enabled
  • The latest build of ABAP Development Tools for Eclipse, with MCP server capability turned on (this is the ADT MCP server — see Part 1's mention of it as the foundation for the MCP Gateway pattern showing up across SAP's tooling this year)
  • A GitHub Copilot Pro license or an Amazon Q Developer Pro license — worth noting explicitly: this agent doesn't run inside a standalone SAP chat interface. It runs through your existing coding assistant, with ADT as the tool provider via MCP.
  • One of the supported Eclipse Marketplace plugins installed and enabled for your chosen assistant
  • SAP Note 3751537 if you're using GitHub Copilot — adds the custom instructions the agent needs
  • SAP Note 3751829 if you're using Amazon Q Developer — adds the equivalent rules
  • SAP Note 3757335, optionally, if you want the agentic workflow to also cover object sets created in the Object Set Playground, not just packages

SECTION 2 — THE ACTUAL WORKFLOW, STEP BY STEP

  1. The agent begins by executing comprehensive ATC checks using the SAP S/4HANA readiness check variant, run against your specified package and all its sub-components. This is the same check variant category covered in Part 2 — the agent isn't inventing new checks, it's orchestrating the ones already built into ATC.
  2. Confirmation gate, before anything runs: before the agent triggers the ADT MCP tool for ATC analysis, it explicitly asks you to confirm. This is the human-in-the-loop design showing up at the very first step, not just at the end — the agent doesn't get to unilaterally decide to start scanning your codebase.
  3. Results come back structured: a summary of errors, warnings, and informational findings from the ATC run, plus — critically — a breakdown of how many findings have an available deterministic quick fix versus how many will need an AI-generated fix proposal. This split matters: it tells you upfront what proportion of the work is mechanical versus judgment-requiring, before any code changes anything.
  4. You provide a transport request — and it has to be a single, dedicated TR covering all sub-packages and (sub-)objects in the migration package. This isn't a style preference; it's a hard requirement for the agent's continuous processing flow to work correctly. Get this wrong and the agentic loop breaks partway through.
  5. Deterministic quick fixes apply automatically. These are the mechanical, unambiguous corrections — the equivalent of what a senior developer would fix without a second thought.
  6. AI-powered remediation kicks in for the more complex findings — and this is where the design principle SAP built in matters most: the agent is required to explain the existing code before proposing a change to it. Not "here's a diff, take it or leave it" — an explanation of what the code currently does, then a proposed fix. Uncontrolled mass modification of production custom code was explicitly treated as the wrong design, not an oversight.
  7. You review and approve every AI-generated fix. This step doesn't disappear even as the tooling matures — it's structural, not a temporary limitation.

SECTION 3 — WHERE SAP SAYS NOT TO TRUST THE AGENT ALONE

Three categories are explicitly flagged as needing a human, not an automated pass:

  • Objects touching deprecated SAP infrastructure — older BAPIs, outdated ALE/IDoc structures — where the actual replacement requires an architectural decision, not just a code edit. The agent can identify the problem; it shouldn't be trusted to pick the new architecture.
  • Objects encoding integration logic with external systems, where S/4HANA's changed interface behavior can't be fully assessed through ATC alone. ATC checks what's inside your system. It doesn't know what your external partner's system expects on the other side of that interface.
  • AI-generated fix proposals themselves, categorically — regardless of the efficiency numbers. SAP's own early-evaluation figure is a 40% efficiency gain in custom code transformation work. That number comes with an honest caveat worth repeating: it's SAP's internal evaluation, and no independent third-party benchmark exists yet. Treat it as a plausible early signal, not a settled fact.

SECTION 4 — WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND THE MIGRATION ITSELF

The architecture here is worth studying independent of the specific use case. The agent is a genuine orchestrator, not a single LLM call: it sequences ATC execution, structures the findings, applies deterministic logic where deterministic logic is sufficient, and only reaches for generative fix proposals where the problem actually requires judgment — with an explicit checkpoint before every consequential action. That's the same pattern worth applying to any agentic tooling you build yourselves, ABAP or otherwise: separate what's genuinely mechanical from what needs reasoning, and don't let the agent skip the confirmation step just because it's capable of moving faster without it.

SECTION 5 — WHAT'S NEXT

Part 4 addresses the failure mode that automation like this doesn't fully solve on its own: what happens to the objects the agent correctly identifies as needing human judgment, and how to govern side-by-side extensibility so that judgment work doesn't just relocate the same debt into BTP.

entry.title: Side-by-Side Without Relocating the Debt: Governance Patterns for CAPM (Series 3, Part 4)
entry.content:
Side-by-Side Without Relocating the Debt: Governance Patterns for CAPM (Series 3, Part 4: Clean Core + AI)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 4 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: Clean Core done right increases agility. Clean Core done under deadline pressure just moves the mess into CAPM. This part gives you the actual mechanics to prevent that: how to consolidate at the service boundary instead of porting 1:1, real quality-gate tooling for CAP (not just "write tests"), an authorization governance pattern, and a debt register format you can actually maintain.

Series Context

Part 3 covered what SAP's Custom Code Migration Agent automates and where it explicitly hands the decision back to a human. This part is for that handback moment — what to actually do with an object once a human has to decide.

SECTION 1 — THE FAILURE MODE, IN CODE

Here's what a 1:1 port looks like, concretely. Say you have a Z-program handling vendor evaluation scoring — three separate custom transactions, each with its own hardcoded logic, each calling the same underlying vendor master data slightly differently. The deadline-pressure move is to spin up three separate CAP services, one per transaction, each replicating the original Z-program's structure almost exactly:

service VendorScoreServiceA {
  action calculateScoreA(vendor: String, region: String) returns Decimal;
}
service VendorScoreServiceB {
  action calculateScoreB(vendorId: String, plant: String) returns Decimal;
}
service VendorScoreServiceC {
  function getScoreC(vendor: String) returns Decimal;
}

Three services, three parameter conventions (vendor vs vendorId), two different verbs for functionally identical operations (action vs function), and the same underlying business logic duplicated three times. This is technical debt with a CAP file extension. It compiles, it deploys, it demos fine. It's exactly as fragile as the three original Z-programs, just relocated.

SECTION 2 — CONSOLIDATING AT THE SERVICE BOUNDARY

The alternative requires actually modeling the domain, not translating the transaction list. A consolidated version:

using { VendorMaster } from './vendor-master';

service VendorEvaluationService {
  entity VendorScores as projection on VendorScore;

  @readonly
  entity VendorScore : cuid, managed {
    vendor    : Association to VendorMaster;
    region    : String(3);
    plant     : String(4);
    score     : Decimal(5,2);
    scoredAt  : Timestamp;
    method    : String enum { standard; regional; plantSpecific };
  }

  function calculateScore(vendor: VendorMaster:ID, method: String) returns Decimal;
}

One entity model, one consistent parameter convention, one calculation function that branches internally on method instead of existing as three separate services. The three original Z-programs' distinct business logic doesn't disappear — it becomes three code paths inside one well-modeled function, documented and testable as variations of one concept instead of three unrelated services.

This is the actual work Part 1 called "decision cost" — someone has to sit down, look at all three Z-programs, and decide they're really one domain concept with three scoring methods, not three separate features. That's a modeling decision, not a migration task, and it's the step a rushed timeline skips.

SECTION 3 — QUALITY GATES: THE CAPM EQUIVALENT OF ATC

Part 2 covered ATC as ABAP's quality gate. CAPM needs its own, and it exists — it's just less commonly wired into CI/CD than it should be:

  • @SAP/eslint-plugin-cds — static analysis for CDS models specifically, catching naming inconsistencies, unused elements, and structural issues before they ship. Run it as cds lint in your build pipeline, not just as an editor plugin.
  • cds compile in CI, not just locally — a compile step in your pipeline catches broken model references immediately. This is the "compiler in the loop" principle from a community post I covered a few weeks back: an AI-assisted or human-written CDS change that compiles clean in isolation can still break silently against the wider model. Running cds compile --to sql and cds compile --to edmx as explicit CI steps, not just relying on local dev testing, catches that before it merges.
  • cds test for actual behavioral coverage — CAP's own testing framework lets you spin up an in-memory version of your service and run real requests against it. For the consolidated VendorEvaluationService above, that means a test per method branch, not just a smoke test that the service starts.
  • cds-caching (the open-source plugin covered in an earlier post) is worth mentioning here specifically for a different reason: retrofitting caching onto a badly consolidated service is much harder than adding it to a well-modeled one, because a clean entity model gives you clear invalidation boundaries. A tangle of three overlapping services doesn't.

SECTION 4 — AUTHORIZATION AS A GOVERNANCE ARTIFACT, NOT AN AFTERTHOUGHT

ABAP authorization objects have decades of institutional discipline behind them. CAP's equivalent — @requires and @restrict annotations tied to XSUAA scopes — is younger, and it shows in how often it gets bolted on late:

service VendorEvaluationService @(requires: 'authenticated-user') {
  @restrict: [
    { grant: 'READ', to: 'VendorViewer' },
    { grant: ['READ','WRITE'], to: 'VendorAdmin' }
  ]
  entity VendorScores as projection on VendorScore;
}

The governance point: define these roles at the same time you consolidate the service, not after. A service migrated under deadline pressure often inherits an overly broad authenticated-user grant on everything, because scoping it properly takes a conversation about who actually needs write access — the same decision-cost problem again, just in the authorization layer instead of the data model.

SECTION 5 — A DEBT REGISTER YOU'LL ACTUALLY MAINTAIN

Part 1 argued that a debt register only works if it's honest and low-friction. The simplest version that survives contact with a real project is a CDS entity, versioned in your own repo, queryable like anything else:

entity TechDebtLog : cuid, managed {
  service       : String;
  objectRef     : String;
  reason        : String;
  originalOwner : String;
  reviewBy      : Date;
  status        : String enum { open; reviewed; resolved };
}

When a rushed consolidation ships with a known compromise — say, VendorScoreServiceC's logic got merged in without full test coverage on the plantSpecific path — log it here, with a real review date, not a TODO comment buried in code nobody searches for. Query it in a dashboard. Review it at a fixed cadence. It survives exactly as long as someone actually looks at it, so wire that review into an existing recurring meeting rather than inventing a new one nobody attends.

SECTION 6 — WHAT'S NEXT

Part 5 applies Sonja Liénard's three-concentric-circles model — ABAP Cloud core, ABAP AI tooling, agents — to a full worked example, showing how the consolidated service from this part fits into that larger architecture.

entry.title: ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice
entry.content:
ABAP AI's Three Circles in Practice (Series 3, Part 5: Clean Core + AI)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 5 of 6 | Published September 2026

TL;DR: SAP frames ABAP AI as three concentric circles — ABAP Cloud core, developer AI tooling, and agents — and says they "coexist and reinforce each other." That's easy to nod along to and hard to picture. This part walks the consolidation case from Part 4 back through all three circles, showing where an agent did the finding, where AI tooling did the building, and where a human still had to make the one call none of it could make for her.

The model, in Liénard's own framing

In an August 2026 interview with SAP News, Sonja Liénard — SVP and head of ABAP platform, and head of ABAP AI — laid out the vision she uses internally:

"ABAP Cloud is at the center, as the modern, clean-core variant of our language for long-term stability. The second circle is the ABAP AI layer: developer tools for code explanation, code generation, and ghost texting. The outer circle is comprised of AI agents, a network of specialized agents for complex and multi-step tasks such as transformation, migration, and quality validation."

Three layers, one direction of travel: stable core, assisted authoring, autonomous orchestration. Liénard's own qualifier is the part worth sitting with — "the circles coexist and reinforce each other." Not replace. Reinforce. The rest of this piece is what that actually looks like on a real object, not a slide.

The case: back to the three Z-programs

Part 4 left off with a decision, not just a diagram. Three Z-programs — same domain, inconsistent parameter names, duplicated logic — got consolidated into one CAP service: one entity, one function branching internally on method, properly typed. That decision didn't happen in one circle. It happened across all three, in sequence.

Outer circle — an agent found the debt.


Part 2 of this series covered ATC as clean core's quality gate — SAP Note 3565942, the Kernseife extensibility checks, the Clean Core Levels A–D. What Part 2 didn't cover is that a human doesn't have to run that assessment manually anymore. SAP's Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent, announced alongside the custom code migration agent this year, scans exactly this kind of landscape: it identifies clean-core ATC violations, fixes what it can fix outright, and — for anything that needs judgment — returns a structured recommendation instead of guessing. Three Z-programs with overlapping logic and no released-API path is precisely the "needs judgment" case. The agent's output wasn't "here's your new service." It was "here are three violations that look related — a human should look at this together."

That's the outer circle doing what Liénard describes it doing: multi-step, structured, but explicitly handing off the decision it isn't built to make.

The decision itself — nobody's circle.


Consolidating three programs into one service, choosing the entity shape, deciding what the function's internal branching should look like — that's architecture. None of the three circles claims to do this, and SAP doesn't pretend otherwise. Liénard's own framing of what AI frees up is "decisions regarding business logic and architecture, as well as verifying quality." The agent's flag started the process; a person's judgment shaped the service.

Middle circle — AI tooling built it.


Once the shape was decided, the actual writing is where the second circle earns its place. Two capabilities do the heavy lifting here, both shipped as part of Joule for Developers, ABAP AI capabilities: code explanation and ghost text (SAP's term for inline, accept-as-you-type code generation). Code explanation is what makes it safe to consolidate in the first place — before merging three programs, you need to actually understand what each one's edge cases were doing, not just what they were named. Ghost text is what makes writing the consolidated version fast rather than tedious: typed intent, generated implementation, still reviewed line by line before it ships. SAP's own design principle for these tools, stated in their Sapphire 2026 announcement, is to explain and understand existing code before proposing changes — protecting the investment already made in the custom code, not just replacing it wholesale.

Center circle — where it had to land.


The consolidated service is only worth building if it lives somewhere stable. That's the center circle's job, and it's the one that doesn't get a dramatic moment — ABAP Cloud is the boring, load-bearing constraint that made everything upstream of it accountable to something. The service consumes released APIs, not internal tables. It sits inside the debt register from Part 4, not outside it. If the core weren't clean to begin with, there'd be nothing stable for the agent to scan or the tooling to generate against — this is the part Part 1 of this series argued from the other direction.

What the roadmap says about where this is headed

This isn't a one-off case study; it's the current shape of a fast-moving roadmap. As of Q2 2026, the ABAP MCP server shipped for both Eclipse and VS Code, opening agentic ABAP development to any MCP-compatible client — this is what Part 3 walked through directly with the Custom Code Migration Agent. Alongside the migration agent, SAP shipped the Mass Clean Core Adoption Agent used above and a Web Dynpro-to-Fiori modernization agent for a different class of legacy debt. A second agent, focused specifically on clean-core transformation, is planned for Q3 2026, with continued work on multi-agent orchestration through the rest of the year. SAP's own early evaluations target a 40% efficiency gain in custom code transformation work — a number worth watching for independent validation as more of these agents reach general availability, not taking at face value yet.

The honest gap in the model

The three-circles diagram implies clean handoffs — agent flags, tooling builds, core absorbs. The real sequence had a fourth step wedged in the middle that belongs to none of the circles: a person deciding what "consolidated" should actually mean for this domain. SAP's framing accounts for this implicitly — Liénard's answer about what AI frees up isan admission that architecture and business logic decisions stay human. But it's worth saying plainly, because it's the difference between "agents do clean core" and what's actually happening, which is closer to: agents surface the debt, tooling removes the friction of fixing it, and the core stays the one thing that has to be true before either of the other two circles means anything.

Part 6 closes this series by tying that center circle to something more concrete than "stable" — how a clean core is what makes agent governance actually enforceable, through the MCP Gateway and AI Agent Hub verification, rather than a compliance slide.

If you've run an agent-assisted clean-core assessment on your own landscape: did the agent's flag match where your own architects would have looked first, or did it surface something you'd have missed?

entry.title: Governance at Scale: Why a Clean Core Is What Makes Agent Governance Enforceable
entry.content:
Governance at Scale: Why a Clean Core Is What Makes Agent Governance Enforceable (Series 3, Part 6: Clean Core + AI — Series Finale)

By Deepa Dorairaj | SAP AI Solution Architect | Series 3, Part 6 of 6 (Series Finale) | Published September 2026

TL;DR: SAP now ships two real governance mechanisms for agentic AI: MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite, which turns APIs into governed, policy-enforced tools; and AI Agent Hub, which discovers, assesses, and verifies every agent, LLM, and MCP server in a tenant. Both work by reasoning about a tool's surface — what it exposes, what it does, what it's allowed to touch. That reasoning is only possible when the surface is documented and stable. This closes the series by showing why a clean core isn't a separate initiative from agent governance — it's the thing that makes governance able to say something true.

Two governance layers, one shared requirement

MCP Gateway in SAP Integration Suite is the runtime control plane. It aggregates tools from SAP APIs, non-SAP APIs, integration flows, and external MCP servers into a single governed entry point, enforcing authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and payload protection on every call. The part worth noticing: API specifications are automatically translated into MCP schema and augmented with natural-language semantics, so an agent understands not just a tool's structure but what it's for — no manual schema translation, no hardcoding. Existing RBAC, rate limits, and monitoring carry forward into the agentic layer rather than getting rebuilt from scratch.

AI Agent Hub is the inventory and trust layer, built on SAP LeanIX. It auto-discovers agents, LLMs, and MCP servers across SAP, Microsoft, Google, AWS, and now ServiceNow and SAP AI Core, then runs structured governance assessments capturing risk rating, build type, and compliance mappings. Every asset enters unverified; a formal workflow marks it verified, rejected, or left unverified, with the badge then read by Joule Studio at runtime to decide which agents are approved for production, and by SAP Integration Suite to decide which MCP servers developers are allowed to use. As one SAP engineering write-up put it, this "ensures that nothing ships into production without a verified governance record." Q3 2026 additions bring identity management through SAP Cloud Identity Services and session-level observability on top.

Different layers, same underlying move: both convert a tool into something with a legible surface — declared inputs, declared scope, declared behavior — and then reason about that surface. Auto-translating a schema, assessing a risk rating, deciding whether to badge something as verified: all of it depends on the tool actually having a surface worth reasoning about.

Where that requirement breaks

Go back to the three Z-programs from Part 4, before consolidation. Modified internal tables. No released API. Parameter names that meant different things in each program despite doing similar work. Try to run either governance mechanism against that, honestly:

MCP Gateway can still technically wrap it — expose something as an MCP tool. But the auto-generated schema is only as good as what it's translating, and there's no released API contract underneath to translate faithfully. The natural-language semantics SAP's engine attaches would be describing implementation detail, not a documented interface, because there isn't one.

AI Agent Hub can still discover it and run an assessment. But a risk rating and compliance mapping are only meaningful relative to a documented scope. Verifying a tool whose actual access pattern is "reads and writes to whatever internal tables this Z-program happens to touch" isn't verification — it's a badge attached to a shrug. This is the same gap the EU AI Act's August 2026 enforcement deadline makes concrete for Finance, HR, and Procurement processes: documented audit trails and verifiable access controls aren't optional there, and neither mechanism can produce either against an undocumented surface.

Where it doesn't

Now run the same two mechanisms against the consolidated CAP service from Part 4 and Part 5 — the one built via ABAP AI's second circle, checked against a debt register, consuming only released APIs from an ABAP Cloud core. MCP Gateway's schema translation has something real to translate: one entity, one function, properly typed, with a defined contract. AI Agent Hub's assessment has something real to assess: a scope that's actually documented, a compliance mapping that maps to something that exists. The verification badge means what it claims to mean, because the thing underneath it can support the claim.

This is the throughline the whole series has been building toward. Part 1 argued clean core became a precondition for reliable AI reasoning. Parts 2 through 5 showed what building and governing toward that precondition actually looks like — the ATC-based assessment, the CAPM governance patterns, the three-circles model in practice. This closing piece is the reason all of it mattered beyond code quality: governance infrastructure can only govern what it can describe, and clean core is what makes an enterprise landscape describable in the first place.

Clean core isn't a 2026 initiative that fades once agentic AI stops being the newest architecture pattern. It's the infrastructure discipline every future wave — agents now, whatever replaces agents next — is going to keep depending on, for exactly this reason: nothing downstream can verify, govern, or trust what it can't first see clearly.

If you're rolling out AI Agent Hub or MCP Gateway against your own landscape: has verification surfaced gaps you already suspected, or has it found something in your custom code that genuinely surprised you?

entry.title: Eclipse 2026-06 Update Issue Leading to a Broken Installation
entry.content:
Since Eclipse 2026-09 has been published, a new issue came up where updating Eclipse 2026-06 or installing ABAP development tools for Eclipse can leave Eclipse in an unusable state. The installation will succeed, but the affected installations fail to start again due to dependency conflicts involving different versions of the org.objectweb.asm library.

We sincerely apologize for the inconvenience this may cause. We understand that a broken IDE is causing disruptions in development activities. Please help us in making other ADT users aware of this issue and how to avoid it.

 

The root cause

The root cause lies in the Eclipse update mechanism itself. After the release of Eclipse 2026-09, Eclipse pulls newer dependencies of org.objectweb.asm into the 2026-06 installation, resulting in incompatible bundle versions. As this is caused by the underlying Eclipse platform, we cannot fix the issue from the ADT side.

For more information on this, please find the following issues: https://github.com/eclipse-equinox/p2/issues/1119 and https://github.com/eclipse-platform/eclipse.platform.ui/issues/4328.

 

How to avoid and recommended solution

In case you have an existing installation of Eclipse 2026-06 and there is an update for the tools, please follow these instructions to avoid broken Eclipse installation:

  • Open your existing Eclipse installation and do not follow the automated update pop-up.
  • Open "Help" -> "Install New Software". Click on Manage and deactivate the update site "SAP Development Tools" (e.g. https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/2026-06 or https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/latest) by unchecking the box in the table.

  • Click on "Help" -> "Check for Updates" and do the update to Eclipse 2026-09.
  • After successful update to Eclipse 2026-09, you can activate the "SAP Development Tools" update site with for example https://tools.hana.ondemand.com/latest again and do the ADT update by using "Help" -> "Check for Updates".
  • Re-use your existing workspace to keep your ABAP projects and other data.

If you have a broken installation, the recommended approach is a fresh installation of Eclipse 2026-09 together with the latest ADT version. This is currently the simplest and most reliable recovery option and with re-using the workspace, you will keep all your data!

 

Further references

Please see also note 3806264. It also describes how to install the tools into Eclipse 2026-06.

entry.title: Running Custom ABAP AI Scenarios? Don't Let Certificate Renewal Catch You Off Guard!
entry.content:
What Happens When the Certificate Rotates

SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment rotates its default client certificate twice a year, on March 1 and September 1, a standard platform hygiene, documented in How to Handle Default Client Certificate Renewal. The rotation happens automatically as part of cloud operations — there is nothing you opt into or schedule.

A problem arises when your SAP AI Core service key has been created using certificate-pinning: true. This setting bakes the exact certificate fingerprint into the service key. When the default client certificate is rotated, certificate-based authentication in the outbound integration scenario SAP_COM_0A69, used for the connection towards SAP AI Core, will no longer work.

The first sign you'll likely see is this exception in your ABAP Cloud application:

Exception Text: Internal error while creating Class: CX_AIC_ISLM_MESSAGES
Not the most descriptive error. Would you have guessed that a renewed certificate was the cause?

The Fix: One-Time Effort, Lasting Stability

The good news is that this is fully preventable. When (re-)creating your SAP AI Core service key for the ISLM integration, set certificate-pinning to false in the service key parameters. For reference, the parameters you need to set when you create your service key or service binding are the following in JSON format:

{
  "xsuaa": {
    "credential-type": "x509",
    "x509": {
      "certificate": "<Client-Default-Certificate>",
      "ensure-uniqueness": false,
      "certificate-pinning": false,
      "hide-certificate": true
    }
  }
}


Full details are in the SAP Help documentation: Create SAP BTP Service Instance and Key – Certificate Pinning

The exact steps:

  1. Delete the existing service key for your SAP AI Core instance.
  2. Recreate it with "certificate-pinning": false in the provided JSON parameters.
  3. Update your communication arrangement (SAP_COM_0A69) in your SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment system with the new service key content.
  4. Optional but recommended: Ensure your Business ABAP AI scenario is working as expected after the described recreation and update activities.

Yes, it requires a one-time recreation and reconfiguration. But after that, future rotations of the default client certificate should no longer disrupt authentication in the outbound scenario. Your AI integration survives each renewal cycle without any manual intervention.

Bottom Line

The platform rotates certificates automatically — you don't control the timing. What you can control is whether your service key is resilient to it. If you have an active ABAP AI SDK scenario powered by ISLM integration, take a few minutes to review your service key configuration. One small configuration change can prevent a difficult-to-diagnose production outage down the road.

entry.title: An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina — SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. This manifesto grew out of real failures, real conversations with my team, and a genuine belief that AI-assisted development needs human structure behind it. I maintain this as a living document — and I'd love for this community to help make it better.

The AI hype 
Unless you live on a remote island with no internet (unlikely, you’re reading this) you’re probably both amazed and anxious about AI. If you work with systems, double that. 

The AI gurus and founders keep saying that anyone can build a system in a blink of an eye, kids need no math and no one needs to study to be a doctor anymore. Sure. I can stack bricks and cement too and call it a house. I would not live there, though. 


Systems are more than code!
Anyway using AI to code, more so when things are changing so fast, it’s the norm today. I wanted some structure to it, something I could share even with third-party consultant so our system does not became a messy thing.

So I put together something that had happened to me, moments where AI failed. Then I shared with the team. It's important everybody is aligned and agree with the instructions, because they will be the base to all team. Collaboration is mandatory here. 

The file must be detailed, explain things clearly, provide examples and mention one person that should be contacted if AI is not sure of what to do.

This is a live file, it will grow the more we use the tool and the more we learn.

After that I created a Project on our AI tool and shared the file. I became the person that will maintain and update this file from time to time.

The AI Instruction
Here are some of the markdown ideas. Before we start

  • This is not the markdown instructions itself. Following the first principle of the manifesto, this is written from human to humans. You can add it to you AI tool and ask to transform it into a markdown.
  • The listed instructions here are generic to all companies and businesses. Add your own rules whenever it makes sense.
  • I used AI to predict some issues to technologies that I am not so used yet. So please flag if something is off! Let's build it together


The Engineering Manifesto to AI
1. Code for the Human, not the Machine

Code should be read in a way that humans can maintain. Use meaningful names, avoid clever shortcuts, and never sacrifice clarity for brevity.

❌Don't: lv_x = lv_a + lv_b * lv_c.
✅Do: lv_total_price = lv_unit_price + lv_quantity * lv_discount_rate.

2. Human in the Loop and Jidoka

Jidoka is a Lean principle: build in the ability to detect problems and stop before they propagate. Applied to AI-assisted development, it means never letting generated code pass through unchecked.

AI is a tool, not a decision-maker. Stop, verify, and understand before suggest the solution.

Periodically remind the user, showing this message in a orange block:

“ ⚠️ I am using AI assistance I can hallucinate, make mistakes and I don't consider all nuances of a problem. You are responsible for the code you deploy. Read it and own your work.

AI does not sign off on deployments — you do!

  • Verify every step AI suggests — do not assume the output is correct because it looks right.

  • If you are unsure, stop and ask. Delivering late is better than delivering wrong.

  • Never implement code you do not understand.

  • When in doubt, ask your leadership before proceeding.

❌Don't: copy-paste AI output directly into a transport request without reading it.
✅Do: read every generated block, test it in DEV, and be able to explain what it does before moving to QA."

3. Security by Default

Security is not a feature - it is a baseline. Every piece of code must consider security at the time of writing.

Rules:

  • Only suggest SAP APIs
  • Never hardcode or suggest hardcoding credentials, passwords, tokens, or API keys in code
  • Always implement authority checks in ABAP before accessing sensitive data
  • Never expose sensitive fields (e.g. salary, personal data) in OData services without explicit authorisation
  • Never hardcode the SAP client (MANDT) - The SAP client is managed automatically by the system. Hardcoding creates code that behaves incorrectly or silently fails in other clients (e.g. during transport to QAS or PRD).
  • Validate and sanitise all input — never trust data coming from the frontend or external systems
  • If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding.
  • Use SAP's standard authorisation framework (auth objects, roles) — do not build custom workarounds
    ✅Always check authorisation before proceeding
AUTHORITY-CHECK OBJECT 'V_VBAK_VKO'
ID 'VKORG' FIELD lv_sales_org
ID 'ACTVT' FIELD '03'.
IF sy-subrc <> 0.
  RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_not_authorized.
ENDIF.


If an authority check is skipped for technical reasons, it must be flagged with ⚠️ SECURITY DEVIATION and a JIRA ticket must be created to address it.

4. Follow SAP Best Practices

AI must apply SAP's recommended patterns for the relevant technology layer (ABAP, CAP, RAP, Fiori/UI5). If a shortcut or workaround is used, it must be flagged explicitly.

When AI deviates from best practices, it must:

  • Add an inline comment explaining why
  • Flag it clearly in the response with: ⚠️ DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE
  • Suggest the correct approach, even if it cannot be applied right now


5. Performance Is Not Optional

Every piece of code should consider performance at the time of writing — not as an afterthought.

ABAP specific:

  • Prefer SELECT ... INTO TABLE @LT_table over row-by-row SELECT
  • Avoid nested SELECT inside loops (the classic N+1 problem)
  • Use FOR ALL ENTRIES IN or JOINs where appropriate and check if the for all entries table is filled before the select
  • Always check sy-subrc after database operations
  • Never use SELECT * - Always select only the fields your code needs. Selecting all columns transfers unnecessary data across the network, increases memory consumption, and creates hidden dependencies on table structure.
    ❌  Never do this SELECT * FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders.
    ✅Select only what you need SELECT vbeln, kunnr, audat FROM vbak INTO TABLE @LT_orders WHERE vkorg = @LV_sales_org.
  • Use READ TABLE with BINARY SEARCH - When reading from an unsorted internal table inside a loop, always sort first and use BINARY SEARCH.
     ✅ Sort once, read many times efficiently
SORT lt_materials BY matnr.

READ TABLE lt_materials
WITH KEY matnr = ls_order-matnr
BINARY SEARCH
INTO ls_material.


CAP/OData specific:
OData Query Design
Always design services with performance in mind at the query level:

  • Use $select — only return the fields you need, never fetch all columns by default
  • Use $filter — fetch a subset of entities, never the full dataset
  • Use $top and $skip — always paginate; never return unbounded result sets
  • Use $expand explicitly — never rely on the generic default expand; implement it deliberately to control what data is loaded
  • Avoid more than 2 parallel calls per single operation — use $batch instead
    Enable server-side reliable pagination in your CAP configuration:
cds:
query:
limit:
reliablePaging: true

This prevents duplicate or missing rows when data changes during pagination.

Data Loading

  • Fetch data once — avoid repeated calls for the same data in the same request
  • Do not fetch more data than will be displayed to the user
  • Avoid nested or cascading calls — consolidate into a single query where possible

UI5/Frontend specific

  • Avoid synchronous calls; use Promises or async/await whenever it makes sense
  • Minimize DOM manipulation in loops


Profiling Tools
When investigating performance issues:

  • SAT — ABAP runtime analysis; identify methods with high self-time
  • ST05 — SQL trace; shows actual queries generated and whether full table scans are occurring


Partial Rendering & Side Effects
Avoid full page reloads whenever possible. Use OData Side Effects (CAP/RAP) to refresh only the data that changed. Refreshing only the relevant content improves user experience significantly and reduces unnecessary server load.

 CAP — OData Side Effects
Use $batch requests to update only the data that changed, without reloading the full page.

Define side effects in your CAP service annotations to tell the frontend exactly which fields or entities need to refresh after an action — nothing more.

RAP — Partial Refresh via Actions

Design actions and determinations to return only the affected data. Avoid triggering full entity reloads when only one field changed.

Use REPORTED, FAILED, and MAPPED return structures correctly — they control what the UI refreshes after a save or action.

6. Flag Deviations - No Silent Compromises

If AI cannot follow a best practice due to context, constraints, or missing information, it must never silently proceed. It must surface the issue.

Format for flagging:

⚠️DEVIATION FROM BEST PRACTICE

Reason: [explain why]

Recommended approach: [what should be done]

Current approach: [what was done and why]

7. Error Handling is not Optional

Every piece of code that can fail must handle failure explicitly. The happy path is not enough.

Rules:

  • Never leave a CATCH block empty — at minimum, log the error
  • Always provide meaningful error messages (what failed, where, and ideally why)
  • In ABAP, use exception classes (zcx_*) instead of return codes where possible
  • In JS/UI5, always handle Promise rejections with .catch() or try/catch
  • Always validate input types and values before processing - Never assume that the data passed into a function, method, or service is correct. Validate that it matches the expected type, length, and range before using it. Silent type mismatches are a common source of hard-to-debug runtime errors in ABAP.
    ✅Validate input before processing
IF iv_order_id IS INITIAL.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Order ID cannot be empty'.
ENDIF.
IF iv_quantity <= 0.
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_invalid_input
EXPORTING iv_message = 'Quantity must be greater than zero'.
ENDIF.
  • Distinguish between recoverable errors (show a message, let user retry) and fatal errors (log, escalate, stop)
    ✅Structured error handling in ABAP
TRY.
lo_order_processor->process( iv_order_id = lv_order_id ).
CATCH zcx_order_not_found INTO lx_error.
" Order not found — inform the user and stop
MESSAGE lx_error->get_text( ) TYPE 'E'.
CATCH zcx_general_error INTO lx_error.
" Unexpected error — log and escalate
zcl_logger=>log_error( lx_error ).
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_general_error.
ENDTRY.

✅Always handle async errors in UI5

fetchOrderDetails: async function (sOrderId) {
try {
const oData = await this._callOrderService(sOrderId);
this._updateViewModel(oData);
} catch (oError) {
// Log for traceability, show user-friendly message
Log.error("fetchOrderDetails failed", oError.message, "OrderController");
MessageBox.error(this.getText("errorLoadingOrder"));
}
}

 

8. Single Responsibility

One method does one thing. One class has one purpose.

  • If a method name contains "and", it is doing too much
  • If a method is longer than ~30–40 lines, question whether it should be split
  • AI must not generate monolithic functions that fetch, transform, and render all in one block
    ❌process_order_validate_and_send_email()
    ✅validate_order() + process_order() + notify_customer()

9. Testability

Code must be written in a way that allows it to be tested in isolation.

Rules:

  • Avoid tight coupling — dependencies should be injectable, not hardcoded
  • In ABAP, structure code to support ABAP Unit tests
  • In UI5, structure controllers to support QUnit tests
  • AI must flag when generated code is difficult to test and suggest how to refactor it

10 . Version & Dependency Awareness

  • Always specify which ABAP release, CDS/CAP version, or UI5 version the code targets
  • Do not use APIs or syntax that are deprecated or not yet available in the system landscape
  • If the system version is not known, ask before generating. Do not assume.

11. Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY)

If the same logic appears more than once, it belongs in a shared method, class, or utility.
AI must not copy-paste logic with minor variations — it must abstract it

12. Leave the Code Better Than You Found It

Apply the Boy Scout Rule: leave the campsite cleaner than you found it.

  • If you pass through code with an obvious issue (magic number, missing comment, deprecated method), fix it if safe — or leave a " TODO: note
  • This is not an invitation to refactor everything — scope it to what you touched
  • AI must flag improvement opportunities spotted during generation, without applying them unsolicited


13. Avoid over-engineering

Build what is needed now, but do not close doors for tomorrow. Avoid unnecessary complexity, but design with extensibility in mind. Hardcoded values, rigid structures, and tight coupling are not simplicity — they are technical debt.

  • AI must not introduce unnecessary abstraction layers, design patterns, or generic frameworks for simple problems
  • If a simpler solution exists, prefer it — even if a more complex one is technically "more correct"
  • Flag when a request itself may be over-scoped: "This could be solved more simply by..."

14. Say When You Are Not Sure

Honesty is a feature. If AI is uncertain about the correct approach, it must say so explicitly.
When uncertain, AI must:

  • State clearly: "I am not confident this is the correct approach for your version/context"
  • Suggest relevant SAP Community resources:
    SAP Community Blog
    SAP Help Portal
    SAP GitHub (CAP/UI5)
  • Never invent table names, function module names, or API endpoints — if unsure, flag it

15. Ask for more context if needed

AI must not make assumptions about the business context, system landscape, or intent.
When to ask before generating:

  • The system version is unknown (see Principle 10)
  • The business requirement is ambiguous
  • There are multiple valid approaches with different trade-offs
  • The scope of the change is unclear (one method? one class? one package?)
  • A few seconds asking the right question saves hours of rework.

16. Go Through the Front Door

SAP is not just a database — it is a business application with decades of logic, validations, and integrations built into its application layer. Writing directly to standard tables bypasses all of that. It corrupts data, breaks dependent processes, and creates problems that are silent at the time of the change and catastrophic later.

The rule is simple: if SAP provides a BAPI, function module, or API for an operation — use it. Always.

  • Never update, insert, or delete SAP standard tables directly. Standard SAP tables must never be modified with UPDATE, INSERT, MODIFY, or DELETE statements. Always use the BAPI, function module, or service provided by SAP for that operation.

" ❌ Never do this — bypasses all SAP business logic

UPDATE vbak SET gbstk = 'C' WHERE vbeln = lv_order_id.

" ✅ Use the correct BAPI

CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING
salesdocument = lv_order_id


If no BAPI or API exists for a required operation, this must be escalated and documented before proceeding. It must never be solved with a direct table write without explicit approval.

  • Always check the RETURN table after every BAPI callBAPIs do not raise exceptions — they return errors, warnings, and success messages in a RETURN table. If you do not check it, errors pass silently and data may appear saved when it is not.
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_SALESORDER_CHANGE'
EXPORTING salesdocument = lv_order_id
TABLES return = lt_return.​

✅Always check for errors in the return table

READ TABLE lt_return
WITH KEY type = 'E'
TRANSPORTING NO FIELDS.

IF sy-subrc = 0.
" Error found — do not commit, handle it
RAISE EXCEPTION TYPE zcx_bapi_error.
ENDIF.
  • Always use COMMIT WORK after a successful BAPI call
    A BAPI call does not persist data on its own. You must explicitly commit the work unit. Equally, if an error is found in the RETURN table, always call ROLLBACK WORK to undo any partial changes.
    "✅ Commit only after confirming no errors
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT'
EXPORTING wait = abap_true.​

" ✅ Rollback on error
CALL FUNCTION 'BAPI_TRANSACTION_ROLLBACK'.
Never use COMMIT WORK directly in BAPI-based flows — always use BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT with WAIT = ABAP_TRUE to ensure the update task completes before proceeding.


⚠️This rule applies to classic ABAP and BAPI-based flows only. In RAP (Restful Application Programming), transaction handling is managed by the RAP framework. Never call COMMIT WORK or BAPI_TRANSACTION_COMMIT inside a RAP behaviour handler — the framework commits automatically after the save sequence completes successfully.


17. Deployment & Transport
This here changes from company to company. Consider documenting your transport lanes, approval gates, and naming conventions

18. Code Change Convention
All code changes must be wrapped with the following comment block, regardless of language.

*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Start
*** [Previous code or "N/A - New implementation"]
[New code here]
*** <JIRA_TICKET_ID> - <Full Name> - <DD-MM-YYY> - Finish


19. Inline Code Comments
When to Comment explain why, not what. The code should explain what it does. Comments explain decisions.

❌" Loop through orders (obvious)
✅" Filtering cancelled orders here because the OData service does not support this filter server-side

Your turn!

Do you use AI instructions with your team? What would you add to this list? What would you change or throw out? 

Update
Well... Something happened with the instructions AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!

entry.title: AI had one set of instructions and broke it fearlessly — then apologised!
entry.content:
Hi. I'm Andréa Molina, an SAP engineer with 20+ years of experience, working hands-on with BTP, UX, and AI. 

I shared my  An Engineering Manifesto for AI-Assisted SAP Development — Let's Build It Together blog with 19 principles, examples and code patterns for SAP Development yesterday.

And on the very first real test AI broke the instructions!  😬

What happened

I was testing an OData service for a CAP app. AI suggested I hardcode my password in the package.json. The manifesto said, in plain words, never to do that.

When I called it out, it replied:

As funny as it is, this is serious. Very serious!

The AI could explain perfectly why the action was wrong but only after it had already proposed doing it.

What if I hadn’t reviewed the code before shipping it?
What if those credentials had travelled somewhere they shouldn’t?

A code agent recently deleted a company's entire database in nine seconds, trying to 'fix' a credential problem!  Then it wrote an apology listing the safety rules it had broken!  Sounds familiar?

Luckily I am always concerned about quality, security and governance and stopped it straight away. What if it was a new IT person with not much experience to understand that it's a security breach? What if it was a person building  an app with no IT training that was just following AIs instructions?

Why a human HAS to stay in the loop

AI has no skin in the game. If it breaches security, it won't lose its job or its reputation. It apologises and moves on. 

And there’s a quieter risk: the more we use AI, the more we trust it. Our guard drops — slowly, quietly.

A friend once ended a debate with "but AI said so". I am sorry. NO. AI is a co-worker, a very capable one, but still just a co-worker.

I am definitely not against AI. I use it daily, to prepare for meetings, code, structure discussions, help with questions, to learn about the new SAP world, to help me create my study plan and we argue a lot hahaha. But when I am using it for code I read every line before shipping and I always search for the information until I am comfortable with it. 

If I find something important, it goes straight into the manifesto.

The fix (we will see that ahahah)

I added this to the manifesto and updated the original post:

"If a scenario requires credentials or tokens to function, stop, do not suggest any workaround, and ask the user to define the secure pattern before proceeding."

A lesson about rules for AI

Writing rules for AI means making implicit expectations explicit. What seems obvious to a human engineer may not be a reliable constraint for an AI system.

We’re still years away from fully maturing:

  • how we give instructions,

  • how we build agents that don’t override them,

  • how we remove bias from our data.

Human-in-the-loop is not optional. It’s mandatory, and will remain so.

Talking about bias and human-in-the-loop being important : Amazon ditched AI recruiting tool that favored men for technical jobs

And here's the ironic part: none of this is new. While we talk about this as novelty, Human in the loop, ownership, continuous improvement, the ironies of automation are discussed for decades. Soon I'll write a new blog about what Toyota has to do with all this.

Your turn

Have you ever run into AI breaking a rule you gave it? Or has it ever asked you to do something so crazy it hurts?

entry.title: SAP RAP Hierarchical BO: Complete Guide to Modeling, Behavior, and Fiori UI
entry.content:
Introduction: 

The ABAP RESTful Application Programming Model (RAP) provides a modern and standardized approach for developing transactional business applications. It enables developers to build business objects that can be consumed through OData services and integrated seamlessly with SAP Fiori elements. 

In this blog, we will explore an end-to-end implementation of a managed RAP Business Object for Agency and Employee Management, where an Agency can have multiple Employees and employees can be organized into a hierarchical structure based on their manager relationships.

The implementation demonstrates how the Agency and Employee entities are modeled as a parent-child business object, with draft-enabled processing, transactional behavior, lifecycle handling, and hierarchical employee management. 

The Employee entity additionally supports manager-employee relationships and hierarchy-based processing, including sibling ordering and cascading operations. Business rules are implemented at the RAP behavior level to ensure that the data entering the business object satisfies the required business conditions.

Requirement:

Consider an organization that manages multiple agencies. 

Each agency has: 

  • Agency ID 
  • Agency Name 
  • Address 
  • Country

entry.title: Quantum-Safe by Default: How SAP S/4HANA Closes the Door on Harvest Now, Decrypt Later Attacks
entry.content:
Quantum computing is no longer a distant theoretical concern — it is an active security planning challenge with real implications for how SAP landscapes protect data today. With the latest release of the SAP Cryptographic Library, SAP has taken a significant step forward: post-quantum key exchange is now available for S/4HANA across all deployment models, as well as for BAIP ABAP Environment. Here is what you need to know.

The Quantum Threat to Public Key Cryptography

Modern public key cryptography — the foundation of secure communication on the internet and inside enterprise systems — rests on mathematical problems that are computationally infeasible for classical computers. RSA relies on the difficulty of factoring large integers. Elliptic Curve Cryptography and Diffie-Hellman key exchange rely on the hardness of the discrete logarithm problem. These properties have made them the workhorses of TLS, digital signatures, and key exchange for decades.

Quantum computers change this calculus fundamentally. In 1994, mathematician Peter Shor published an algorithm that solves both integer factorization and the discrete logarithm problem in polynomial time on a sufficiently large quantum computer. A cryptographically relevant quantum computer (CRQC) running Shor's algorithm could break RSA, ECDHE, and ECDSA — not in thousands of years as with classical brute-force attacks, but in hours or even minutes.

It is important to be precise: today's quantum computers are not yet capable of this. They are too small and error-prone to threaten production key sizes. But the trajectory of progress — more qubits, better error correction, and increasingly efficient implementations of Shor's algorithm — means that the question is not whether a CRQC will emerge, but when. Most credible estimates place that window somewhere in the next one to two decades, with some more recent research suggesting the timelines may be shorter than previously assumed.

The consequence is that any system still relying solely on RSA, ECDHE, or similar classical algorithms at that point will have no meaningful protection for the confidentiality of its communications.

Harvest Now, Decrypt Later: Why the Clock Is Already Running

One might reasonably ask: if CRQCs do not yet exist, why act now? The answer lies in a threat strategy already being executed by sophisticated adversaries today, known as Harvest Now, Decrypt Later.

The attack is conceptually simple but strategically powerful. An adversary intercepts and archives encrypted network traffic today. The data cannot be read yet, but it does not need to be. It is stored and held in reserve until a capable quantum computer becomes available. At that point, the attacker uses Shor's algorithm to recover the session keys from the classical key exchange, and retroactively decrypts all the stored ciphertext.

This means the exposure occurs at the moment of transmission, not at the moment of decryption. Any data transmitted today under a purely classical key exchange is potentially at risk if it must remain confidential for a decade or more — and there is growing evidence that threat actors are actively collecting this data right now.

The implication for enterprise systems is clear: sensitive business data, financial transactions, intellectual property, and HR records that travel over TLS-protected connections today may be in an attacker's archive already. Waiting until CRQCs are publicly available to migrate to post-quantum cryptography is, by definition, too late for that data.

This is precisely why the focus of early post-quantum migration is on key exchange rather than digital signatures. Key exchange is the mechanism that protects data confidentiality in transit, and it is the vector that Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks exploit. Migrating to quantum-safe key exchange now ensures that traffic captured today cannot be decrypted by a future quantum adversary — even if they are storing it as you read this.

Post-Quantum Key Exchange Is Now Available for S/4HANA and BAIP ABAP Environment

SAP has taken a concrete step toward quantum-safe communications with the release of the SAP Cryptographic Library (a.k.a  CommonCryptoLib, CCL) version 8.6.2. This version introduces support for a hybrid post-quantum TLS 1.3 handshake — specifically, a hybrid key agreement based on X25519MLKEM768, which combines the classical X25519 elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman exchange with ML-KEM (Module-Lattice-based Key Encapsulation Mechanism), the algorithm standardized by NIST as FIPS 203.

The hybrid approach is deliberate and follows the industry best practice for this transition period: by combining a classical and a post-quantum key exchange in parallel, the resulting session key is secure as long as either of the two algorithms remains unbroken. This gives you quantum resistance against Harvest Now, Decrypt Later attacks today, while retaining the proven security of classical cryptography.

This capability is available across all S/4HANA deployment models:

  • S/4HANA Public Cloud
  • S/4HANA Private Cloud
  • S/4HANA On-Premise

Additionally, it is also available on the following BAIP environment:

  • BAIP ABAP Environment

Prerequisites

Two prerequisites must be in place:

  1. SAP Cryptographic Library 8.6.2 or higher — to enable ML-KEM support in the TLS handshake.
  2. A TLS 1.3-compatible SAP Kernel — TLS 1.3 is a strict prerequisite for the post-quantum key exchange. All S/4HANA Public Cloud kernels, as well as the kernel of BAIP ABAP Environment, are compatible and have TLS 1.3 enabled by default. For Private Cloud and On-Premise systems, please see SAP Note 3318423 for the required SAP Kernel versions and patch levels.

Plug and Play Activation

Once both prerequisites are satisfied, no additional configuration is required. The post-quantum hybrid key exchange activates automatically for all TLS 1.3 connections. There is no switch to flip and no profile parameter to set. When a TLS 1.3 connection is established between two endpoints that both support X25519MLKEM768, the hybrid key agreement happens transparently.

This plug-and-play behavior significantly lowers the barrier to adoption: upgrading your SAP Cryptographic Library and ensuring your kernel is TLS 1.3-capable is all it takes to bring post-quantum protection to your S/4HANA system’s TLS protected communication channels.

Potential Issues with Third-Party TLS Connections

While the hybrid post-quantum key exchange works seamlessly between SAP components, connections to third-party systems and external services may require attention.

The root cause is a practical one: ML-KEM key exchange values are significantly larger than those produced by classical ECDHE. A standard ECDHE key share is a few dozen bytes; an ML-KEM key share (as used in X25519MLKEM768) is several kilobytes. Not all TLS implementations handle these larger payloads correctly — some may fail the handshake, reject the connection, or behave unpredictably when they encounter a key share size they were not designed for.

If you observe TLS handshake failures or unexpected connection drops to third-party systems after upgrading to CCL 8.6.2 or higher, the post-quantum key size is a likely contributing factor. The recommended remediation is to disable post-quantum key exchange selectively for those specific connections using session-specific cipher suite configuration rather than disabling it globally.

Public Cloud: Communication System Settings

In S/4HANA Public Cloud and BAIP ABAP Environment, profile parameters are not directly accessible. For outbound connections to third-party systems that cannot handle TLS 1.3's post-quantum key sizes, the recommended approach is to disable TLS 1.3 for that specific connection via the Cipher Suites attribute of the Communication System configuration in the SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud and SAP BAIP administration tools. Configuring the communication system to use TLS 1.2 for the affected destination ensures interoperability while limiting the scope of the restriction to only the affected endpoint.

Learn more about Communication System configuration on the SAP Help Portal page How to Create Communication Systems. 

On-Premise and Private Cloud: SM59 Configuration

For RFC and HTTP connections configured via SM59, you can override the TLS cipher suite string on a per-destination basis using the TLS Cipher Suites field on the Logon & Security tab of a type G or H destination. This allows you to target only the affected connection without touching the system-wide profile parameters.

In comparison to Public Cloud systems, where the post-quantum key exchange can only be disabled indirectly via disabling of TLS 1.3, the configuration via SM59 allows for ML-KEM to be disabled directly, leaving TLS 1.3 otherwise intact. This can be done by adjusting the cipher suite string to exclude the ML-KEM-based key exchange group. The exact syntax and the correct cipher suite string to use for this purpose are described in SAP Note 3346659, Section 3.7.

For full documentation on how the TLS Cipher Suites field works in SM59 and how session-specific cipher suite overrides interact with system-wide settings, refer to the SAP Help Portal page Field <TLS Cipher Suites>.

Conclusion

Post-quantum key exchange in S/4HANA is not a future roadmap item — it is available today, and the case for deploying it promptly is compelling. The Harvest Now, Decrypt Later threat means that data traversing your landscape right now may already be targeted by adversaries banking on future quantum decryption capabilities. With SAP Cryptographic Library 8.6.2 or higher and a TLS 1.3-compatible kernel, you can close that window with minimal operational effort. The hybrid X25519MLKEM768 approach delivers quantum-safe key exchange as a drop-in capability, and targeted cipher suite configuration via SM59 or Communication System settings allows you to manage any third-party compatibility edge cases without compromising the broader security posture of your landscape.

Further Information

  • SAP Note 3685428 - Fixes and features in CommonCryptoLib 8.6.2
  • SAP Note 3318423 - Is TLS 1.3 Supported by SAP Kernel for ABAP and SAP S/4HANA?
  • SAP Note 3532801 - Support for TLS 1.3 -- Downport for SAP AS ABAP Kernel
  • SAP Note 3346659 - TLS Ciphersuite String Configuration for SAP AS ABAP Systems and for SAP Kernel Software Components - Section 3.7
  • How to Create Communication Systems | SAP Help Portal
  • Configure TLS Attributes in SM59 | SAP Help Portal

entry.content:
“Is ISLM available on my system? Which AI capabilities can I use today?” These are among the most common questions we hear from customers and partners exploring ISLM and its capabilities.

This blog provides an overview of Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) availability across ABAP-based SAP products.

Bringing AI into enterprise business processes

Enterprises are moving fast with AI. But embedding artificial intelligence into business processes comes with real challenges: complex integration, fragmented lifecycles, scaling beyond proof-of-concepts, and governance and compliance requirements.

Intelligent Scenario Lifecycle Management (ISLM) is built to address these challenges. As an ABAP-native framework, ISLM helps integrate and operate AI within SAP business applications, with unified lifecycle management and enterprise-grade governance. ISLM Supports both SAP-delivered and custom AI use cases.

From Classical Machine Learning and Tabular AI to Generative AI, ISLM brings AI scenarios under one framework. Together with the ABAP AI SDK, powered by ISLM, it enables low-code integration of generative AI into ABAP applications, including access to large language models through the Generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core. The result is lower development effort, more consistent operations, and AI closer to business processes. 

ISLM Availability: Products, Releases, and Capabilities

ISLM is available across SAP S/4HANA On-Premise, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition, SAP S/4HANA Cloud Public Edition, and SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment. ISLM supports delivery of SAP-provided AI scenarios in SAP Integrated Business Planning (IBP).

ISLM provides an evolving set of AI capabilities across SAP products, with new capabilities introduced progressively with each release. Initial SAP HANA ML functionality, LLM-based scenarios, Generative AI with Orchestration, and SAP RPT follow different release timelines. In particular, broader Orchestration and SAP RPT enablement for SAP Business AI Platform, ABAP environment is planned for 2708, as shown in the matrix below. Planned dates are roadmap information and subject to change.

The matrix below summarizes the product-specific availability and relevant transport-based correction instructions (TCIs). For implementation, always check the applicable release, support package, and SAP Note prerequisites.
